::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Shortest distance between parabola and point](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2815493/shortest-distance-between-parabola-and-point), asked by [Po Chen Liu](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/427093/po-chen-liu) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2018-06-11; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> > Find the shortest distance between the parabola defined by $y^2 = 2x$ and a point $E:= (1.5, 0)$.
>
> I can't use the distance formula because I'm missing a set of points $(x, y)$ to plug into. So, instead, I have a normal that passes through the point $E$ from the parabola. Which is the definition of the shortest distance to a point.
>
> $$y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$$
>
> The slope of the normal is $\frac{1}{y_1}$ by using implicit differentiation and that's where I'm stuck, because I plug the point E into it and I get
>
> $$y_1^2=x_1-1.5$$
>
> How do I prove the shortest distance is $\sqrt{2}$?
:::

A reply to an old comment brought me back here, and I noticed that no one had offered a Lagrange multiplier solution.  You're looking for the minimum of
$$f(x,y) = (x-1.5)^2 +y^2$$
subject to the constraint that $g(x,y) = 0$, where
$$g(x,y) = y^2-2x$$
The critical points satisfy $\nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y)$ for some $\lambda$.  Or,
$$\begin{align*}
    2x-3 &= -2\lambda \\ 2y &= 2 \lambda y
\end{align*}$$
The second of these implies either $y=0$ or $\lambda = 1$.  If $y=0$, then $x=0$ and $f(0,0) = \frac{9}{4}$.  If $\lambda = 1$, we can substitute it into the first equation and get $x = \frac{1}{2}$.  If $x =\frac{1}{2}$, then $y = \pm 1$, and $f(\frac{1}{2},\pm1) = 2$.  So the minimum value of $f$ is at these two points, and the shortest distance is $\sqrt{2}$.
